items.title: Joseph Daley interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, March 18, 2018
items.q: I mean going back to like Mingus, instead of having an icon like Mingus would just draw a casket and say pass it on... But other times he would just draw an image or he would make a political statement... So he would do it on that level if it needed to be done that way.

ctx.x: With a graph of a sort. And is that sort of your blueprint so to speak? And at first I just thought that was interesting. And then coupled with a composed melody that you and Scott eventually would join together on. And I just wanted to comment on that. I thought that was interesting. You sort of invented a way to get your ideas across.

Yeah. Well I didn’t invent that. I mean the graphic scores have been used for years and years and years. Graphic scores are basically an eye concept that many musicians — I mean going back to like Mingus, instead of having an icon like Mingus would just draw a casket and say pass it on. This is what I want. I want you guys to sound like this. And it would be like a casket, you know, something that would kind of like push you into another emotional level. Because the concept in music is to get off of the page. You…

band. They plot them out through the graphic score like that where this person’s at the 15 yard line, then he goes this and then he goes up. And this icon comes around and it forms this beautiful whatever, this formation. So the same type of thing with me. I take these icons and I move them along, and then I want a certain textorial formation set up. And the musician sees the exact texture that I want set up.
